title: Built-in types
hook: The runtime gives you integers, IEEE floats, `decimal`, `bool`, `char`, `string`, and friends. For grades and money, `decimal` is the type; `double` is for science and graphics.

sections.heading: Pick the numeric type on purpose
sections.prose: `int`/`long`/`byte` and unsigned variants are exact integers. `float`/`double` are binary floating point — `0.1 + 0.2` is the same family of error as JavaScript `number`. `decimal` is a 128-bit decimal type for base-10 fractions: currency, GPA, CSV percent columns. It is slower and larger; that is the trade. `bool` is not an int. `char` is a UTF-16 code unit. `string` is an immutable reference type. `object` is the CTS root. `dynamic` is a separate topic. Date/time (`DateTimeOffset`) and `Guid` are BCL structs you will use as if they were built-in.

snippets.label: decimal grades vs double pixels
snippets.explanation: Interview answer: double for measurements and Skia; decimal for anything you would print as currency or a report card. JS has no decimal primitive — you fake it with libraries or integers of cents.

interviewTakeaways: `string` is a reference type; `int` and `decimal` are value types.
`bool` does not convert to `int` implicitly (unlike C).
commonPitfalls: Using `float` for money because JSON numbers look like floats.
Parsing CSV scores into `double` then rounding in surprising ways.
Assuming `char` is a full Unicode scalar — surrogate pairs need `string` or `Rune`.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS `number` is double. `bigint` is integers only. C# splits int/long/double/decimal as first-class types.
